item.title: We Have A Situation
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description:
Franklin Delano Roosevelt rubbed his eyes, leaning back against the leather of his chair. It was late afternoon in 1933, and the Oval Office was stifling, thick with the scent of wool suits, damp rain, and fresh ink. Between navigating bank panics and drafting initial New Deal legislation, it had been a brutal, exhausting day.

The heavy oak door swung open, but it wasn’t his trusted secretary, Louis Howe. A woman stepped inside wearing a sharp, dark pantsuit, tapping frantically on a glowing rectangle of glass. “Mr. President, we have a situation,” she said, her voice laced with urgent authority. “The Chief of Staff needs you in the Situation Room immediately. Things are escalating quickly in Germany.”

item.title: The Blessing
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description:
Marcus woke at dawn, as he always did, kneeling beside his bed before his feet ever touched the cold floor. The apartment was small—barely more than a studio—but the morning light filtering through the single window held a quality that felt almost sacred.

“Lord,” he whispered, hands clasped, “bless me with work today. Provide for Your humble servant.”

It was a ritual he’d kept for three years now, ever since losing his job at the factory. Not a prayer of desperation anymore, but one of gratitude. He’d learned that much. Even now, scraping by on gig work, he had shelter. He had breath in his lungs. That was enough.

item.title: The Test
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description: The workshop at the bend of the Tiber sounded like no other place in the Roman Empire. It did not ring with the chaotic, uneven beat of hammer on anvil, but with the rhythmic, clockwork thrum of water-driven cams and precision-turned gears. Outside, dozens of hopeful young men lined the dusty stone path—sons of senators, scholars, and wealthy merchants, all desperate to study under the enigmatic Architectus, the man who had single-handedly revolutionized construction, irrigation, and metallurgy across Italy.

item.title: The Long Game
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description: The morning fog over the pines at Zavidovo was thick enough to swallow the birch trees whole. George Bush adjusted the collar of his woolen sweater, staring out the floor-to-ceiling window of the state dacha. Outside, the air was bitter cold, but inside, the modern Soviet retreat burned with quiet, prosperous warmth. This wasn’t the decaying, bureaucratic empire his predecessors had anticipated decades ago. The Soviet Union in the winter of 1990 was modern, sleek, and dangerously confident—a market-socialist leviathan that had successfully retooled its central planning without surrendering an inch of its global reach.

item.title: The Duplicate
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description: The thin handles of the plastic grocery bag dug painfully into my fingers, carrying nothing more than a cheap box of coffee filters. Ten minutes. I had been gone for ten minutes. Yet as I pushed open the front door, the air inside felt instantly, terrifyingly wrong. The deadbolt was unlatched. From the kitchen, the familiar sizzle of searing garlic drifted down the hallway, wrapped in the warm, careless laughter of my wife and daughter.

item.title: The Ashworth Manor Murder
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description:
Rain hasn’t let up all night, and neither has the phone. When it finally rings past midnight, it’s Inspector Hale, and his voice has that particular flatness that means someone’s dead. Ashworth Manor. Come now.

You find Lord Ashworth slumped over his study desk, a shattered brandy glass at his elbow and no sign anyone forced their way in. Hale’s already pinned a scrap of corkboard to the wall — a tangle of string leading nowhere, evidence of a trail he couldn’t follow. “I know who was in this house tonight,” he says, “I just can’t prove who left last.” He hands you the thread. The rest is yours to trace.

item.title: Galactic Hegemony
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description: Emperor Valerius awakened to the gentle, rhythmic hum of a captive singularity suspended beneath his bedchamber. Five thousand years after humanity learned to fold the fabric of space like silk, physical scarcity had vanished from the universe. Entire stars were siphoned for minor energy grids; quantum matter-synthesizers rendered rare elements as common as dirt. Yet as Valerius stepped onto his balcony overlooking the capital-spire—a ring-world structure encircling three star systems—he knew the bitter truth of his age: resources were infinite, but human greed remained limitless.

item.title: The Efficiency Paradox
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description: Dr. Marcus Chen had spent three years building the case, and now it sat compiled in a single folder on his laptop: California, if it seceded tomorrow, would be the second-richest nation on Earth, trailing only the United States itself. Not oil. Not tourism. Governance. Fifteen years ago, the state had folded artificial intelligence into the machinery of administration — permitting, budgeting, infrastructure routing, even judicial scheduling — and the results were undeniable. Wait times for permits had dropped from months to hours. The state budget, once a battlefield of pork and gridlock, balanced itself with surgical precision. Roads got built. Wildfires got predicted and starved of fuel before they could spread. It was, by every metric Marcus could measure, the most efficient government in human history.

item.title: Red Horizon
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description:
Month six of nine, and the Meridian hummed along its long arc toward Mars like a held breath. Five crew, four hundred systems, three redundancies for every one that mattered — and still the ship found ways to bite.

First it was a coolant loop tripping offline for no reason anyone could find. Then a scrubber cycling into fault mode at 3 a.m., waking the whole crew to the smell of stale recycled air. Then a comms blackout that lasted six hours and left everyone staring at a silent console, waiting for a voice that didn’t come.

item.title: A Mercedes in Detroit
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description:
INTERNAL MEMORANDUM — FORD MOTOR COMPANY

Piquette Avenue Plant, Detroit, Michigan

TO: Mr. Henry Ford

FROM: Chief Engineer, Special Projects Division

RE: Findings — Unidentified Motorcar, Recovered October 1913

CLASSIFICATION: Confidential

Mr. Ford,

As instructed, my team has spent the past eleven days disassembling the automobile recovered from the roadside near Woodward Avenue. I regret to inform you that our findings have raised more questions than they have answered, and I confess a measure of professional humility I have not felt since my apprentice days.
